explanations.answer: Bring them to Jerusalem as prisoners
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. Saul wants the letters so that “…he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.” The letters are for the synagogues in Damascus, but the trip back is meant to end in Jerusalem. This is a heavy part of the story, so I'm just going to say it plainly.

explanations.answer: Drive them out of the city
explanations.explanation: That one sounds close, but it isn't what the text says. Saul isn't trying to run anyone out of Damascus. He wants to bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. Different direction, friend, and a much heavier plan.

explanations.answer: Put them on trial in Damascus
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a trial in Damascus. Saul's plan is to find them and bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. Damascus is where he looks, and Jerusalem is where he's taking them. This is a heavy part of the story, so I'm just going to say it plainly.

I see why you'd lean that way, but the verse is wider than that. Saul is looking for “…any men or women belonging to the Way…” Women are right there in the text. That's what makes this such a heavy road he's walking.

That's right, it's false. The verse says Saul wants to find “…any men or women belonging to the Way…” Nobody gets skipped on his list. The Way is what the writer calls the group of Jesus' followers here.

Yes, Jesus is the One speaking, and He says, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” Saul calls Him Lord before he even knows the name. Imagine asking a question and getting the BEST answer, and also the one you did not plan for. I bet Saul's whole walk was rearranged in one sentence.

Gabriel is a fair guess. He's an angel who says he stands in the presence of God (Luke 1:19). But the voice on the road doesn't name an angel. Jesus is the One who answers Saul: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…”

Elijah was a prophet of Israel, and he did hear from God (1 Kings 18:36). But Saul's question gets a different answer on this road. Jesus is the One who replies, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” No guessing needed, friend.

explanations.answer: He will be told what he must do
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “…go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” Notice He doesn't hand Saul the whole plan on the road. Saul gets one step, which is get up and go. Some days that's all any of us get, and honestly it's a lot.

explanations.answer: He will meet the high priest there
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say anything about the high priest in this part. He tells Saul, “…you will be told what you must do.” The only instruction Saul gets is to get up and go into the city. That's the whole assignment for now, friend.

explanations.answer: He will be put on trial there
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about a trial. He tells Saul to get up and go into the city, and that he will be told what he must do. No courtroom, no judge, just a next step. It sounds a lot calmer than what Saul had planned for other people.
Speechless is the word. The men “…stood there speechless.” They heard the voice but did not see anyone. I think I'd have lost my words too, because there's no good line for that moment.
The text doesn't say they were weeping. It says they stood there speechless. They heard the voice, but they did not see anyone. Words just left the building.
Rejoicing isn't what the text gives us. It says the men stood there speechless. They heard the voice but did not see anyone. Speechless is the word to hold on to, friend.
Right, they “…led him by the hand into Damascus.” Remember, Saul set out breathing murderous threats and asking for letters. Now he's being led along by the hand. That's quite a switch.

The text doesn't have a mat in this scene. Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could not see a thing. So the men led him by the hand into Damascus. No mat anywhere in the story, friend.
No donkey in the text, friend. Saul got up from the ground, and the men led him by the hand into Damascus. I think a donkey might have been a smoother ride, but that's my guess, not the text.

That's right. “For three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything.” That comes after the men led him by the hand into Damascus. Three days with no sight and nothing to eat or drink is a long stretch. I'd be talking to my empty cookie jar by hour two.

It's actually true, and the verse is plain about it. “For three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything.” The writer doesn't say how Saul felt about it. All we know is that he went through it.

explanations.answer: A man from Tarsus named Saul
explanations.explanation: Yep. The Lord says to ask for “…a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying.” Ananias gets a street, a house and a name. That's a clear set of directions, even if the destination is a lot to take in.

explanations.answer: A man from Cyprus named Barnabas
explanations.explanation: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36), so the pick makes sense. But the Lord sends Ananias to ask for “…a man from Tarsus named Saul…” Different hometown and different name, friend.

explanations.answer: A man from Cyrene named Simon
explanations.explanation: Simon of Cyrene is the man who was made to carry Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21). He isn't who the Lord sends Ananias to find. The Lord says to ask for “…a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying.”

That's the one. The Lord says Saul has seen “…a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” So the Lord tells Ananias about his own part in what Saul saw. That's a lot to hear about yourself in one vision.
The vision isn't about reading anything. The Lord says Saul saw Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight. Scripture isn't part of what the Lord describes.
Saul's men are the ones who led him by the hand into Damascus. The vision the Lord describes is different. Saul sees Ananias place his hands on him to restore his sight.

You got it. Ananias says, “And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” He lays out the whole situation to the Lord. That's right there in verse 14, in his own words.

It's actually true. Ananias says, “…he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” That's right there in verse 14, in his own words. He spells it out to the Lord.

That's what the Lord says. Saul will carry His name “…before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.” Gentiles means people who aren't Israelites. That's a big, wide assignment for a man who had asked for letters to arrest followers of the Way.

The Lord doesn't name priests and elders here. He says Saul will carry His name “…before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.” The people of Israel are one group He names, and the Gentiles and their kings are the other. That's a much wider reach than a single group.

The disciples in Damascus are already followers. The Lord says Saul will carry His name “…before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.” That's a much longer road than one city.
It's actually false. The Lord says, “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” That's a plain look at what's ahead, right alongside the calling. The Lord doesn't hide it.

That's right, it's false. The Lord says, “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” So the calling and the suffering are spoken together. That's a heavy line, so I'll let it stand as it is.
Yes. Ananias says, “Brother Saul.” Just a few verses ago he was telling the Lord about all the harm this man had done. Now he walks in and calls him brother. That is a whole lot of road in one word.
Master is a title for someone above you, and Ananias doesn't use it. He says, “Brother Saul.” He stands beside Saul, not below him.
Teacher would be a respectful word, but it isn't the one in the text. Ananias says, “Brother Saul.” He's greeting Saul as family, with his hands already on him.
It's actually false. The verse says, “At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored.” No waiting, no slow fade. It all happened at that instant.

That's right. The text says “At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored.” Not little by little, not over the next few days. After three days in the dark, the light just came back.
That's right. After his sight is restored, “He got up and was baptized…” Notice the order: his sight comes back, and then he gets up and is baptized. It's the next thing the text tells us he does.
It's actually true. The text says, “He got up and was baptized…” That comes right after his sight is restored. Read verse 18 again, friend, and it's right there.

That's the word. Saul “…spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.” The same Damascus disciples he came to arrest are now the ones he's sitting with. I'd love to have seen that first handshake.
Pharisees aren't who the verse names. It says Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus. The people he came to arrest are the ones he stays with. That's quite a change of company.

The verse doesn't say elders. It says he “…spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.” These are the same followers of Jesus he came to take as prisoners. The text doesn't tell us what was said, so I'll leave that open.
